A magnetic compass has been demonstrated in 18 species of migrating birds. In all species studied with regard to its functional properties, it was found to be an ‘inclination compass’, i.e. the birds derive directional information from the inclination of the field lines, and thus distinguish between ‘poleward’ and ‘equatorward’ rather than ‘north’ and ‘south’. Such a mechanism means that birds from the northern and southern hemisphere may rely on the same migratory programme. Long-distance migrants, however, face the problem that their magnetic compass gives bimodal information at the magnetic equator. Transfers of information between the magnetic field and celestial sources of directional information have been demonstrated; the two systems interact in a complex way. The data on the use of magnetic parameters for position finding are less clear. The experiments involve releases of homing pigeons; correlations of their orientation with natural variations in the magnetic field and the effects of magnetic manipulation reveal an enormous variability. The role of magnetic parameters in the multifactorial navigational system is poorly understood. Keywords: geomagnetic field, compass orientation, ‘inclination compass’, homing, navigational ‘map’ The magnetic field of the earth The geomagnetic field is a dipole field whose poles lie in the vicinity of the geographic (rotational) poles. The field lines leave the ground at the antarctic pole, then curve around the earth and re-enter its surface at the arctic pole, i.e. the magnetic vector points upwards in the southern and downwards in the northern hemisphere, being parallel to the earth’s surface at the magnetic equator (Fig. 1). The angle between the magnetic vector and the horizon is called inclination or dip; lines of equal inclination run roughly parallel to the lines of equal latitude. Magnetic north and geographic north mostly differ by a certain number of degrees. This deviation, declination or variation, may be considerable near the magnetic poles, but it soon becomes negligible at lower latitudes. In most parts of the world, the field lines run roughly south–north. The total intensity of the field decreases gradually – roughly symmetrically in both hemispheres – from maximum values of about 60 000 nT at the poles to about 30 000 nT near the magnetic equator. Extended deviations from the ideal values show continent-wide patterns; different degrees of magnetization of rock units cause local magnetic anomalies, which, however, rarely exceed 1000 nT. Temporal variations of the geomagnetic field occur on a daily, on a secular and on a geological time scale. The latter two types of changes are so slow that they have to be taken into account only in evolutionary considerations. The regular daily variations, in contrast, mostly in the range 30–100 nT, and irregular fluctuations associated with magnetic storms (characterized indicated by K-values, a geomagnetic index, see Lincoln, 1967) are important for all considerations of a navigational ‘map’ (see below). A detailed description of the geomagnetic field and its variations in time and space was given by Skiles (1985). Because of its structure, described above, the geomagnetic field represents a very reliable, omnipresent source of information. The magnetic vector provides directional information, and the spatial distribution of factors such as total intensity and inclination may provide information about position. fetched_contents.text: The sun compass revisited Abstract Many animals, and birds in particular, are thought to use directional information from the sun in the form of a time-compensated sun compass, with predictably deviated orientation under clock shift being regarded as the litmus test of this. We suggest that this paradigm obscures a number of other ways in which solar-derived information could be important in animal orientation. We distinguish between the known use of the sun's azimuth to provide absolute geographical direction (compass mechanism) and its possible use to detect changes in heading (heading indicator mechanism). Just as in an aircraft, these two kinds of information may be provided by separate mechanisms and used for different functions, for example for navigation versus steering. We also argue that although a solar compass must be time-referenced to account for the sun's apparent diurnal movement, this need not entail full time compensation. This is because animals might also use time-dependent solar information in an associatively acquired, and hence time-limited, way. Furthermore, we show that a solar heading indicator, when used on a sufficiently short timescale, need not require time compensation at all. Finally, we suggest that solar-derived cues, such as shadows, could also be involved in navigation in ways that depend explicitly upon position, and are therefore not strictly compass-related. This could include giving directionality to landmarks, or acting as time-dependent landmarks involved in place recognition. We conclude that clock shift experiments alone are neither necessary nor sufficient to identify the occurrence of all conceivable uses of solar information in animal orientation, so that a predictable response to clock shift should not be regarded as an acid test of the use of solar information in navigation. Keywords: avian navigation, clock shift, compass orientation, heading indicator, shadows, solar cues, time-compensated sun compass Highlights * • Sun compasses may be fully or only partially time compensated. * • Navigational uses of noncompass solar information are explored. * • The sun may be used as a heading indicator without time compensation. * • Solar time-dependent place and landmark recognition are explored. * • Clock shift is an ambiguous test of sun compass orientation. ---------------------------------------- The finding that birds use a time-compensated sun compass for orientation is one of the great enduring discoveries of animal navigation research (Kramer, 1950, 1952; Schmidt-Koenig, 1958). Although not the only compass that birds use, the sun compass appears to be dominant in diurnal species. As a very distant but highly visible object, the sun can provide reliable compass guidance because its geographical direction effectively does not change as the animal's position changes. However, the Earth's spin produces an arc of apparent movement of the sun across the sky through the day, and this means that the sun's geographical direction does change slowly through time. The same holds true for its attendant directional cues such as polarization patterns or shadows (Chappell & Guilford, 1995). Insects have long been known to use sky polarization patterns in orientation (Reppert, Gegear, & Merlin, 2010; Wehner, 1998), and there is growing evidence that birds, and other vertebrates apart from mammals, may do so too (Muheim, 2011). Remarkably, birds appear capable of learning enough about the pattern of the sun's directional movement through the day to compensate for it, and hence to use the sun as a compass. The time-compensated sun compass enjoys an unchallenged position at the centre of our understanding of bird navigation, where, in combination with large-scale map factors, it is thought to control navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process (Baker, 1978, 1984; Kramer, 1961; Wallraff, 2005; Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 2009). It is also thought to be important in homing from familiar sites (Fuller, Kowalski, & Wiltschko, 1983; Luschi & Dall'Antonia, 1993), and even in fine-scale orientation tasks such as food storing (Sherry & Duff, 1996; Wiltschko & Balda, 1989; Wiltschko, Balda, Jahnel, & Wiltschko, 1999) and laboratory maze learning (Budzynski, Dyer, & Bingman, 2000; Chappell & Guilford, 1995; Zimmerman, Nicol, & Guilford, 2009). Central to inferring the operation of a time-compensated sun compass is the clock shift (or phase shift) procedure, in which animals that have had their endogenous diurnal clock phase-shifted predictably misinterpret the geographical direction of the sun and orient in a direction appropriate to their own shifted subjective time (Wallraff, 2005; Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 2009). Evidence for the use of time-dependent solar cues in orientation has been found in many other taxa, including frogs (Landreth & Ferguson, 1968), turtles (DeRosa & Taylor, 1978; Graham, Gergoes, & McElhinney, 1996), lizards (Adler & Philips, 1985), rodents (Fluharty, Taylor, & Barrett, 1976; Haigh, 1979), sandhoppers (Pardi & Grassi, 1955; Ugolini, Melis, Innocenti, Tiribilli, & Castellini, 1999) and insects (Lepidoptera: Perez, Taylor, & Jander, 1997; Reppert et al., 2010; Hymenoptera: Wehner & Müller, 1993). Although we frame our argument here in relation to birds, the ideas that we develop are sufficiently general that they should also apply to other taxa. Fundamentally, this is an ideas paper in which we revisit the sun compass concept and suggest that while birds almost certainly do use a time-compensated sun compass in the classical sense, this does not exclude the possibility that they use solar cues in other ways for orientation. Some other uses of solar cues have been proposed previously. fetched_contents.text: Landscape complexity influences route-memory formation in navigating pigeons Abstract Observations of the flight paths of pigeons navigating from familiar locations have shown that these birds are able to learn and subsequently follow habitual routes home. It has been suggested that navigation along these routes is based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks. Previous research has identified the effect of landmarks on flight path structure, and thus the locations of potentially salient sites. Pigeons have also been observed to be particularly attracted to strong linear features in the landscape, such as roads and rivers. However, a more general understanding of the specific characteristics of the landscape that facilitate route learning has remained out of reach. In this study, we identify landscape complexity as a key predictor of the fidelity to the habitual route, and thus conclude that pigeons form route memories most strongly in regions where the landscape complexity is neither too great nor too low. Our results imply that pigeons process their visual environment on a characteristic spatial scale while navigating and can explain the different degrees of success in reproducing route learning in different geographical locations. Keywords: pigeon, navigation, homing, familiar area, landmark, vision 1. Introduction Pigeons have long served as a model for the study of avian navigation, and it is known that they can make use of some form of navigational map, probably based on atmospheric odours, combined with time-compensated solar compass information, in a two-step process, to orient homeward from distant unfamiliar places [1]. Once pigeons become familiar with their environment, however, they are thought to resort to the second mechanism of homing, involving memorized local features [2]. The nature of this familiar area map has received far less attention until recently, with the dominant finding being that pigeons released repeatedly from the same site have been observed to form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft [3–5], which they are attracted back to and faithfully recapitulate even if released a short distance from the original site [4], strongly suggesting the use of familiar visual cues. Route formation and route fidelity vary greatly, however, within individual routes, between individuals, between sites and even between lofts [6,7], but the cause of this variation is not understood. Here, we attempt to improve our understanding of the phenomenon by investigating the relationship between the route-memory formation and visual information complexity of the underlying landscape. Previous analyses of the relationship between these memorized flight paths and the landscape have indicated a preference for prominent linear features in approximately the homeward direction [3,4,8,9]. A naive hypothesis might argue that the bird's ability to determine its position and required direction should increase monotonically with the amount of visual information available, leading to faster learning of the memorized route and greater fidelity in recapitulation. Supporting this idea, previous studies have found that birds are attracted to edge-containing locations in the landscape and change their flight behaviour significantly when approaching them [10]. However, experiments by Wiltschko et al. [11] and Schiffner et al. [7] have indicated that pigeons may be unable to form a memorized route in a highly urban environment (suburban Frankfurt, Germany). Visual inspection of the positions of probable landmarks in our previous research [12] has also suggested that pigeons may form fewer memories in highly urban areas. Such environments provide a wealth of visual information, but theoretical neural-network models have suggested that excessive information may lead to confusion and difficulty in route learning [13]. This poses the question of whether there is an optimal density of information in the landscape over which a bird is homing for the formation or processing of visual memories. We approach this problem by analysing how the route fidelity varies in relationship to underlying landscape complexity over different stages of the route-learning process. 2. Experimental procedures Using micro-GPS devices attached to the birds’ backs, we recorded the flight paths of pigeons repeatedly released from one of four release sites in the Oxford area, indicated in figure 1a. Every bird was initially naive and was released a total of 20 times from its selected release site. This research was conducted in accordance with UK animal welfare legislation and the most recent edition of the ASABs Guidelines for the treatment of animals in behavioural research and teaching. (b). Estimating visual information We defined the amount of visual information in the landscape by the local density of edges in an aerial image. We used the canonical Canny edge-detection filter [14] to identify edges. We then took localized averages of the number of pixels containing edges at each point in the image. We performed this averaging over a range of scales from 100 to 500 m to ensure that our results were not sensitive to a particular visual range of the birds. (c). Calculating route fidelity We defined the route fidelity of a bird by the average proximity of one flight path to that immediately preceding it. For every pair of successive paths, we calculated the nearest-neighbour distance (NND) from every point on the first path to its closest neighbouring point on the second path. Smaller distances between successive paths indicate greater fidelity to a memorized path. (d). fetched_contents.text: Magnetic storms disrupt nocturnal migratory activity in songbirds Abstract Birds possess a magnetic sense and rely on the Earth's magnetic field for orientation during migration. However, the geomagnetic field can be altered by solar activity at relative unpredictable intervals. How birds cope with the temporal geomagnetic variations caused by solar storms during migration is still unclear. We addressed this question by reproducing the effect of a solar storm on the geomagnetic field and monitoring the activity of three songbird species during autumn migration. We found that only the European robin reduced nocturnal migratory restlessness in response to simulated solar storms. At the same time, robins increased activity during early morning. We suggest that robins reduced activity at night when the perception of magnetic information would be strongly disrupted by temporal variations of the magnetic field, to extend their migration during daytime when several visual cues become available for orientation. The other two species, chiffchaff and dunnock, showing low or no nocturnal migratory activity, did not respond to the solar storm by changing activity. Keywords: animal navigation, bird migration, magnetic compass, migratory restlessness, compass orientation, geomagnetic field 1. Background The Sun's energy flux shows periodic variations with longer intervals of low energy and shorter intervals with high energy that are defined as solar storms [1]. The high-energy ions emitted during solar storms interact with the ionosphere causing temporary alterations of the geomagnetic field with stronger effects at higher latitudes [1,2]. Songbirds possess the ability to detect and use the geomagnetic field for orientation during migration [3,4], but it is not clear if they are able to tell apart the spatial characteristics and the temporal variations of the magnetic field [5]. A magnetic map based on the combination of geomagnetic intensity and inclination may affect orientation [3], ecophysiology [6,7] and activity [8,9] in bird migrants. Furthermore, local geomagnetic anomalies caused by the characteristics of the Earth's crust can disrupt birds' navigation ability [10,11]. Effects of temporal variability caused by solar activity on the geomagnetic field have already received some attention in different organisms (see references in [2]), but less is known about the effects on birds [12–14]. We tested three species of migratory songbirds, two of which are expected to migrate at night (chiffchaff Phylloscopus collybita; European robin Erithacus rubecula) and one that migrates during the day (dunnock Prunella modularis). We monitored their activity in cages for several days while exposed to geomagnetic displacements using either constant values or variable magnetic parameters that simulated the effect of a solar storm. 2. At the time of capture, all birds had finished their post-juvenile moult and, with one exception, had started to accumulate fat. Birds were kept indoors in individual cages for a few days until the start of the experiments, at which time they were provided with food and water ad libitum. We randomly divided each species in two groups of four individuals. Each group was assigned to one of six identical experimental houses [7], and introduced in the cages in the afternoon of the day preceding the start of the experiment. The houses were built in non-magnetic material with semi-transparent roofs that exposed the birds to natural light conditions without providing any external visual cues (i.e. Sun position, stars motion or the skylight polarization pattern) [7]. All experiments were carried out 13–27 October 2017, after which all birds were released nearby. (b). Each house was equipped with an Axis P1427-LE network camera that continuously recorded the four cages from above [9]. Branch report on the core navigation systems birds use for direction and location

Migratory birds use a combination of primary navigation systems to determine direction and location, with the most well-supported systems being a magnetic compass, a time-compensated sun compass, and learned landmarks or scenery-based route memory. The evidence indicates that the magnetic field is a central orientational cue, with birds using it to determine direction and, in some contexts, position. A review explicitly states that a magnetic compass has been demonstrated in 18 species of migrating birds and describes it as an “inclination compass,” meaning birds derive directional information from the inclination of field lines rather than just magnetic north/south [N2-F1]. This same source also notes that magnetic compass orientation is only one part of a multifactorial navigational system, with transfers of information between magnetic and celestial cues demonstrated in complex ways [N2-F1]. 

For celestial cues, the evidence points to the sun compass as a dominant orientation system, especially in diurnal birds. The sun compass is described as a “time-compensated sun compass,” with predictable deviations under clock shift regarded as a major discovery in animal navigation research [N3-F2]. The source explains that the sun provides reliable compass guidance because its geographical direction does not change with the animal’s position, but its apparent movement through the day requires compensation. The bird’s ability to compensate for this movement is key to using the sun as a compass, and the evidence suggests that solar-derived cues may also function as heading indicators or even contribute to place recognition and landmark guidance [N3-F2]. A broader review also states that migratory birds use both celestial and geomagnetic directional information to orient on their way between breeding and wintering areas [N2-R2]. This indicates that celestial cues are not separate from magnetic cues but are integrated as part of a larger orientation system.

The third core system is landmarks and learned scenery, particularly route memory. The evidence here emphasizes that navigation along habitual routes may be based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks [N4-F3]. Pigeons are presented as a model system that can use memorized local features once they become familiar with their environment [N4-F3]. The same source argues that pigeons may form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft, which they recapitulate even after being released from a short distance from the original site [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that route memory is an important component of navigation, especially for shorter, repeated trips. The evidence also notes that route fidelity is influenced by landscape complexity, with pigeons forming route memories most strongly in landscapes of moderate complexity rather than too simple or too complex [N4-F3]. This suggests that landmarks and scenery are not just passive cues but are actively processed in a way that depends on environmental structure.

How compass-based orientation differs from route-based navigation is that compass-based systems provide directional heading information, while route-based navigation relies on memory of landmarks and scenery to refine the path. The compass systems are more general and can operate over long distances, whereas route-based navigation is typically used in familiar areas and becomes more prominent after birds become accustomed to a location [N4-F3]. The evidence also supports the distinction between a map-like navigational system and a route-based system: pigeons are described as using a navigational map combined with solar compass information for long-distance homing, but then resorting to memorized local features once they become familiar [N4-F3]. This implies that compass orientation gives the broad direction, while route memory provides the fine-scale details needed to follow a specific path.

How birds combine different cues to maintain heading and position is central to the evidence. The review states that magnetic and celestial cues interact in a complex way, with transfers of information between them demonstrated [N2-F1]. The sun compass review explicitly states that the time-compensated sun compass is thought to control navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process [N3-F2]. This means that birds do not rely on one cue alone; instead, they integrate compass cues with map-like information to control direction. The same source also suggests that solar cues can have multiple roles, including heading indicators and time-dependent place recognition, which broadens the ways cues are combined [N3-F2]. The route-memory study shows that pigeons combine compass and landmark guidance in familiar route navigation [N4-R4], indicating that multiple cues are used in parallel rather than sequentially. The evidence therefore supports a multimodal navigation strategy: birds integrate magnetic, solar, and landmark information, with each cue contributing to heading, position, or route refinement depending on the context [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Branch report on disturbances and failures that can disrupt navigation

Common natural and human-made disturbances to bird navigation include geomagnetic disturbances, solar activity, weather, light pollution, and magnetic interference. The evidence is strongest for geomagnetic disturbances and solar-related geomagnetic variability. One source states that geomagnetic disturbances affect the navigation of both young birds and their elders, suggesting that birds rely similarly on geomagnetism [N5-R1]. Another study reports that geomagnetic disturbances are associated with increased incidence of wrong-way bird migrations [N5-R4], while a review of magnetic storms notes that solar activity can alter the geomagnetic field at unpredictable intervals, disrupting temporal geomagnetic variations during migration [N5-F4]. This indicates that natural disturbances, especially those linked to solar storms and geomagnetic changes, are a major source of navigation failure.

Weather and light pollution also disrupt navigation. Although the provided evidence is thinner on weather effects than on geomagnetic ones, the general point is clear: environmental conditions can interfere with orientation. The review on magnetic storms notes that geomagnetic variability can disrupt the perception of magnetic information during migration [N5-F4]. Light pollution is not explicitly detailed in the evidence set, but the broader context of celestial cues and the sun compass implies that artificial light can disrupt nocturnal orientation. The sun compass review notes that the sun’s apparent movement requires compensation, and that clock shift experiments are ambiguous indicators of sun compass use [N3-F2]. This suggests that any disruption to the circadian system or to the sky’s visible structure—such as artificial light—could interfere with celestial orientation.

Magnetic interference is another major disturbance. The evidence shows that geomagnetic anomalies and magnetic field irregularities can disrupt navigation. The magnetic orientation review states that local geomagnetic anomalies caused by the Earth’s crust can disrupt birds’ navigation ability [N2-F1], and the magnetic storms study notes that geomagnetic displacement and temporal variation can affect orientation [N5-F4]. In other words, birds are sensitive to both the main magnetic field and its local variations, and any interference with those signals can impair navigation.

How weather, light pollution, and magnetic interference affect orientation is not fully spelled out in the evidence provided, but the available material does support the following conclusions. Geomagnetic disturbances and solar storms can disrupt the magnetic information birds use, leading to misorientation and altered migration behavior [N5-F4]. Magnetic anomalies can disrupt navigation ability locally [N2-F1]. Weather-related geomagnetic variability can disrupt the perception of magnetic information during migration [N5-F4]. The evidence also suggests that birds may reduce activity under conditions when magnetic information is disrupted, as the European robin reduced nocturnal migratory restlessness in response to simulated solar storms [N5-F4]. This implies that birds do not always maintain orientation under disturbance; instead, they may alter their behavior, such as shifting activity to daylight when magnetic cues are unreliable [N5-F4].

What happens when navigation cues are unreliable or missing is that birds may drift off course, take wrong-way routes, or fail to maintain consistent heading. The evidence shows that geomagnetic disturbances can cause wrong-way migrations [N5-R4], and that birds may rely on the same geomagnetic cues even when displaced, suggesting that cue loss can force them to rely more heavily on other cues or to become disoriented [N5-R1][N5-F4]. The review on magnetic orientation notes that the role of magnetic parameters in navigation is poorly understood, with experiments revealing enormous variability and the need for magnetic recalibration [N2-F1]. This suggests that when magnetic cues are unreliable, birds may either compensate poorly, fail to recalibrate, or depend more heavily on other cues, which may not be sufficient to restore accurate navigation. Overall, the evidence supports a picture of navigation as fragile: birds can be thrown off course by geomagnetic disturbances, solar storms, or magnetic anomalies, and when cues are missing or inconsistent, orientation becomes less reliable and migration can go awry [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-F4][N2-F1].
node_outputs.N9:
Branch report on environmental cues that guide and stabilize bird navigation

Magnetic fields, solar position, and star patterns provide directional information in different ways. The magnetic field is described as an omnipresent, reliable source of orientational information, with birds using it as a magnetic compass to distinguish between poleward and equatorward directions rather than purely north and south [N2-F1]. The same review explains that the magnetic vector provides directional information, and spatial factors such as total intensity and inclination may provide position-related information [N2-F1]. This means that magnetic cues are not only directional but also contribute to positional awareness. For solar cues, the evidence is especially strong: birds use a time-compensated sun compass, and the sun is regarded as a central orientation cue because its geographical direction does not change with the animal’s position [N3-F2]. The sun compass review further notes that birds may also use solar cues as heading indicators and that solar-derived cues such as shadows could be involved in navigation in ways that depend on position, including giving directionality to landmarks or acting as time-dependent landmarks involved in place recognition [N3-F2]. For star patterns, the evidence is less detailed than for the sun compass, but it does confirm that birds use the stars as a compass and that the star compass, like the sun compass, is not innate and must be learned through observation of the rotating sky [N3-R1]. This suggests that stellar cues contribute to directional information, especially for nocturnal navigation.

Landmarks and scenery help birds refine their route by providing familiar visual cues that pigeons and other birds can use to navigate successfully from previously visited places [N4-F3]. The evidence states that navigation along habitual routes may be based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks, and that pigeons can form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft [N4-F3]. Route memory is also linked to landscape complexity: pigeons form route memories most strongly in regions with moderate landscape complexity, and the study concludes that pigeons process their visual environment on a characteristic spatial scale [N4-F3]. This indicates that landmarks and scenery are not just passive cues but are actively used to stabilize route fidelity. The evidence also supports the idea that route memory is combined with compass guidance, with pigeons relying on both landmark and landscape features in familiar route navigation [N4-R4]. Therefore, landmarks and scenery refine navigation by allowing birds to adjust heading and stay on a specific path after they have learned the route.

Which cues are used at different migration stages and distances is supported by the evidence in several ways. Long-distance migration is associated with a combination of map-like navigational systems and compass orientation. The review on magnetic orientation says that birds are sensitive to the Earth’s magnetic field and its variations, and that magnetic compass orientation is part of a multifactorial navigational system [N2-F1]. It also notes that the use of magnetic parameters for position finding is less clear, suggesting that magnetic cues are especially useful for broad orientation rather than for precise location [N2-F1]. The sun compass review describes the time-compensated sun compass as central to navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process [N3-F2]. This suggests that celestial cues are especially important during long-distance or unfamiliar navigation, where birds must combine compass information with map-like information. For route fidelity and learned routes, the evidence points to landmark and scenery-based navigation becoming more prominent once birds become familiar with an area [N4-F3]. The review on pigeons states that once pigeons become familiar with their environment, they resort to memorized local features, indicating that learned route memory is more relevant for short-distance or familiar-route navigation [N4-F3]. Taken together, the cues used at different stages appear to shift from broad compass and map-based orientation during long-distance migration toward landmark and route memory when birds are navigating from familiar places [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

Branch report on how birds learn routes and use memory during migration

Birds form and use memory for familiar routes and landmarks through a process that involves repeated travel, experience, and visual learning. The evidence shows that pigeons are able to learn and subsequently follow habitual routes home, with navigation along these routes based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks [N4-F3]. The study also notes that pigeons may form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft, which they recapitulate even after being released from a short distance from the original site [N4-F3]. This strongly supports the idea that route memory is not just a single waypoint memory but a learned path that can be recalled repeatedly. # Integrated final answer: how birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration

Bird migration is a highly precise ecological phenomenon that depends on a combination of innate compass systems, learned route memory, and environmental cues. Birds do not rely on a single mechanism; instead, they use a multifactorial navigation system in which different cues are integrated depending on the migration stage, distance, and environmental conditions [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence supports a picture of migration as a layered process: broad compass and map-like orientation guide long-distance navigation, while landmarks and scenery stabilize familiar routes and refine heading [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

## 1) Which primary navigation systems do birds use?

The core systems identified in the evidence are:

- **A magnetic compass**  
  Birds use the Earth’s magnetic field as a directional cue. A review explicitly states that a magnetic compass has been demonstrated in 18 species of migrating birds and describes it as an “inclination compass,” meaning birds derive directional information from the inclination of field lines rather than purely magnetic north/south [N2-F1]. The same source notes that magnetic compass orientation is part of a multifactorial navigational system, with transfers of information between magnetic and celestial cues demonstrated in complex ways [N2-F1]. This indicates that the magnetic compass provides broad directional orientation rather than precise location alone.

- **A time-compensated sun compass**  
  The sun is another major orientation system, especially in diurnal birds. The evidence states that birds use a time-compensated sun compass, with predictable deviations under clock shift regarded as a major discovery in animal navigation research [N3-F2]. The review explains that the sun provides reliable compass guidance because its geographical direction does not change with the animal’s position, but its apparent movement through the day requires compensation. Birds appear capable of learning enough about the sun’s directional movement through the day to compensate for it, and the sun compass is thought to control navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process [N3-F2]. This means the sun compass is especially useful for large-scale orientation and heading control.

- **A star compass and learned landmarks/scenery**  
  The evidence also supports the use of stellar cues and learned visual landmarks. The star compass, like the sun compass, is not innate; birds must observe the rotating sky to develop it [N3-R1]. Landmarks and scenery are used for route refinement. The route-memory study states that navigation along habitual routes may be based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks, and pigeons can form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft [N4-F3]. Pigeons are also described as using memorized local features once they become familiar with their environment, and route fidelity varies with landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This shows that learned route memory becomes especially important for familiar areas and short-distance navigation.

## 2) How do compass-based orientation and route-based navigation differ?

Compass-based orientation and route-based navigation serve different navigational functions:

- **Compass-based orientation** provides broad directional heading. It relies on cues such as magnetic inclination, solar position, and celestial cues to maintain overall direction. The evidence indicates that magnetic compass orientation gives poleward/equatorward information, while the sun compass helps birds compensate for the sun’s apparent movement [N2-F1][N3-F2]. This system is useful for long-distance migration and unfamiliar navigation.

- **Route-based navigation** relies on memory of landmarks and scenery to refine the path. Once birds become familiar with an area, they resort to memorized local features rather than relying solely on compass cues [N4-F3]. This means route memory is not a substitute for compass orientation; it is a refinement mechanism that helps birds stay on a specific path after they have learned it.

The distinction is important because birds do not switch between one system and the other in isolation. Instead, the evidence suggests that compass orientation gives the general direction, while landmarks and scenery stabilize the route and allow birds to adjust heading when they are near home [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3]. The review also notes that the role of magnetic parameters in position finding is poorly understood, and that experiments reveal enormous variability, which underscores the complexity of integrating multiple cues [N2-F1].

## 3) How do birds combine different cues to maintain heading and position?

Birds combine cues in a multimodal, interrelated way. The evidence shows that magnetic and celestial cues interact in complex ways, with transfers of information between them demonstrated [N2-F1]. The sun compass review explains that the time-compensated sun compass is central to navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process, and that solar cues may also function as heading indicators or even contribute to place recognition [N3-F2]. This means that birds do not treat each cue as a separate system; instead, they integrate compass information with map-like information to control direction and position.

The route-memory evidence supports the same idea. Pigeons combine compass and landmark guidance in familiar route navigation [N4-R4]. This indicates that multiple cues are used in parallel rather than sequentially. The study also shows that pigeons process their visual environment on a characteristic spatial scale and that route fidelity is influenced by landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This suggests that cue integration is not only about combining compass and landmark information, but also about tuning that combination to the local environment.

The broader evidence on cue integration also implies that birds reduce error by using multiple cues. Although the evidence provided is thinner on this point than on the specific cue systems, the contextual material on multimodal navigation indicates that navigation is multi-modal, and birds may use different cues at different times in response to environmental conditions [N6-R2]. In other words, birds compensate for uncertainty by relying on a combination of cues rather than a single one.

## 4) What environmental cues guide and stabilize bird navigation?

Birds use a hierarchy of cues that guide and stabilize migration:

### a) Magnetic fields  
The magnetic field is an omnipresent, reliable source of orientational information [N2-F1]. Birds use it as a magnetic compass to distinguish between poleward and equatorward directions, and the geomagnetic field is described as a compass cue in Cataglyphis ant navigation [N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that magnetic parameters may provide position-related information, though the use of magnetic information for position finding remains less clear [N2-F1]. This means magnetic cues are important for both heading and, to some extent, position, especially over long distances.

### b) Solar position  
The sun is a dominant orientation cue, especially for diurnal birds. The time-compensated sun compass is described as a central orientation system, and the sun’s geographical direction does not change with the animal’s position [N3-F2]. The review also notes that solar-derived cues may function as heading indicators and that shadows can contribute to navigation in ways that depend on position [N3-F2]. This means solar cues are especially useful for maintaining heading and for fine-scale navigation.

### c) Star patterns  
The evidence shows that birds use stars as a compass, and the star compass is not innate but must be learned through observation of the rotating sky [N3-R1]. While the evidence is less detailed than for the sun compass, this still supports the idea that stellar cues are an important directional cue, especially for nocturnal navigation.

### d) Landmarks and scenery  
Landmarks and scenery stabilize familiar routes. The evidence states that navigation along habitual routes may be based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks, and pigeons can form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft [N4-F3]. Route memory is also linked to landscape complexity: pigeons form route memories most strongly in regions with moderate landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This means that landmarks and scenery are not just passive cues; they are actively used to refine the path and maintain route fidelity.

## 5) Which cues are used at different migration stages and distances?

The evidence supports a staged navigation strategy:

- **Long-distance migration and unfamiliar navigation** rely heavily on map-like compass systems. The magnetic orientation review says that birds are sensitive to the Earth’s magnetic field and its variations, and that magnetic compass orientation is part of a multifactorial navigational system [N2-F1]. The sun compass review describes the time-compensated sun compass as central to navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process [N3-F2]. This suggests that long-distance migrants use broad compass and map-like information to maintain direction over large distances.

- **Familiar-route navigation** relies more on learned landmarks and scenery. Once birds become familiar with their environment, they resort to memorized local features [N4-F3]. Pigeons are described as using memorized local features once they are familiar with their surroundings, and their route fidelity is influenced by landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This indicates that learned route memory becomes more prominent when birds are navigating from places they have visited before.

- **Route fidelity and memory formation** depend on repeated travel and experience. The evidence shows that pigeons are released repeatedly from the same site and that this repeated exposure leads to the formation of memorized paths [N4-F3]. Route fidelity varies greatly within individual routes, between individuals, between sites, and even between lofts [N4-F3], showing that memory formation is shaped by experience rather than being fixed.

## 6) What disturbances can disrupt navigation?

Bird navigation is vulnerable to several disturbances:

### a) Natural disturbances  
Geomagnetic disturbances are a major concern. The evidence states that geomagnetic disturbances affect the navigation of both young birds and their elders, suggesting that birds rely similarly on geomagnetism [N5-R1]. It also reports that geomagnetic disturbances are associated with increased incidence of wrong-way bird migrations [N5-R4]. A magnetic storm study notes that solar activity can alter the geomagnetic field at unpredictable intervals, disrupting temporal geomagnetic variations during migration [N5-F4]. This means that birds can be thrown off course by geomagnetic variability.

### b) Weather and magnetic interference  
Weather-related geomagnetic variability can disrupt the perception of magnetic information during migration [N5-F4]. Magnetic anomalies caused by the Earth’s crust can also disrupt navigation ability [N2-F1]. The evidence suggests that birds may reduce activity when magnetic information is disrupted, as the European robin reduced nocturnal migratory restlessness in response to simulated solar storms [N5-F4]. This indicates that birds do not always maintain orientation under disturbance; instead, they may alter behavior when cues are unreliable.

### c) Human-made and light-related disturbances  
Although the evidence is thinner on light pollution than on geomagnetic disturbances, the broader context of celestial cues and the sun compass implies that artificial light could disrupt nocturnal orientation. The sun compass review notes that clock shift experiments are ambiguous indicators of sun compass use [N3-F2], which suggests that disruptions to circadian or sky-based cues can interfere with navigation. The evidence also implies that light pollution may disrupt nocturnal orientation by altering the availability or reliability of celestial cues [N3-F2].

### d) What happens when cues are unreliable or missing  
When navigation cues are unreliable or missing, birds may drift off course, take wrong-way routes, or fail to maintain consistent heading. The evidence shows that geomagnetic disturbances can cause wrong-way migrations [N5-R4], and that birds may rely on the same geomagnetic cues even when displaced, suggesting that cue loss can force them to rely more heavily on other cues or to become disoriented [N5-R1][N5-F4]. The review on magnetic orientation also notes that the role of magnetic parameters in navigation is poorly understood, with experiments revealing enormous variability and the need for magnetic recalibration [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that navigation becomes less reliable when cues are inconsistent, and that birds may fail to recalibrate or compensate effectively under disturbance.

## 7) How do birds learn routes and use memory during migration?

Birds learn routes through repeated travel and experience. The evidence shows that pigeons are able to learn and subsequently follow habitual routes home, with navigation along these routes based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks [N4-F3]. The study also notes that pigeons may form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft, which they recapitulate even after being released from a short distance from the original site [N4-F3]. This indicates that route memory is not just a single memory but a learned path that can be recalled repeatedly.

Repeated travel and experience are critical to route fidelity. The evidence indicates that pigeons are released repeatedly from the same site and that this repeated exposure leads to the formation of memorized paths [N4-F3]. Route fidelity increases with repeated release, and the study reports that route formation and route fidelity vary greatly within individual routes, between individuals, between sites, and even between lofts [N4-F3]. This suggests that experience shapes memory formation, and that route memory is strengthened by repeated exposure.

Landscape complexity affects route memory and navigation by determining whether memory can be formed and retained effectively. The evidence shows that pigeons form route memories most strongly in regions where landscape complexity is neither too great nor too low [N4-F3]. The study concludes that pigeons process their visual environment on a characteristic spatial scale and that landscape complexity is a key predictor of fidelity to the habitual route [N4-F3]. This means that overly complex landscapes may overwhelm the bird’s memory system, while overly simple landscapes may not provide enough structure to support route learning. The evidence also notes that pigeons are attracted to strong linear features in the landscape, such as roads and rivers, and that landmarks influence flight path structure [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that landscape complexity influences which landmarks become salient and how effectively a route can be remembered and followed.

## 8) Integrated conclusion

In ecology, birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration through a combination of innate compass systems, celestial cues, and learned route memory. They use the magnetic field as a compass to distinguish direction, the sun as a time-compensated compass to maintain heading, and stars as a nocturnal compass [N2-F1][N3-F2][N3-R1]. Landmarks and scenery provide route refinement and familiar navigation, especially once birds become accustomed to an area [N4-F3]. Birds also integrate cues across stages: long-distance migration depends on map-like orientation, while familiar routes depend on memory of landmarks and scenery [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

Disturbances such as geomagnetic storms, solar variability, magnetic anomalies, weather, and artificial light can disrupt navigation by degrading cue reliability or making cues unavailable [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-F4]. When cues are unreliable or missing, birds may fail to maintain heading, drift off course, or take wrong-way routes [N5-R4][N5-F4]. Learning and memory are therefore critical: repeated travel strengthens route memory, and birds’ ability to remember familiar routes depends on the structure of the landscape and the balance between too much and too little visual information [N4-F3].

Overall, bird migration is a sophisticated ecological achievement that depends on a flexible, multimodal navigation system, with cues selected and integrated depending on the migration stage, distance, and environmental conditions [N2-F1][N3-F2][N6-R2]. Birds do not rely on a single cue; they combine compass, celestial, and learned route information to achieve precise navigation during migration.

# Integrated final answer: how birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration

Bird migration is a highly precise ecological phenomenon that depends on a combination of innate compass systems, learned route memory, and environmental cues. Birds do not rely on a single mechanism; instead, they use a multifactorial navigation system in which different cues are integrated depending on the migration stage, distance, and environmental conditions [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence supports a picture of migration as a layered process: broad compass and map-like orientation guide long-distance navigation, while landmarks and scenery stabilize familiar routes and refine heading [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

## 1) Which primary navigation systems do birds use?

The core systems identified in the evidence are:

- **A magnetic compass**  
  Birds use the Earth’s magnetic field as a directional cue. A review explicitly states that a magnetic compass has been demonstrated in 18 species of migrating birds and describes it as an “inclination compass,” meaning birds derive directional information from the inclination of field lines rather than purely magnetic north/south [N2-F1]. The same source notes that magnetic compass orientation is part of a multifactorial navigational system, with transfers of information between magnetic and celestial cues demonstrated in complex ways [N2-F1]. This indicates that the magnetic compass provides broad directional orientation rather than precise location alone.

- **A time-compensated sun compass**  
  The sun is another major orientation system, especially in diurnal birds. The evidence states that birds use a time-compensated sun compass, with predictable deviations under clock shift regarded as a major discovery in animal navigation research [N3-F2]. The review explains that the sun provides reliable compass guidance because its geographical direction does not change with the animal’s position, but its apparent movement through the day requires compensation. Birds appear capable of learning enough about the sun’s directional movement through the day to compensate for it, and the sun compass is thought to control navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process [N3-F2]. This means the sun compass is especially useful for large-scale orientation and heading control.

- **A star compass and learned landmarks/scenery**  
  The evidence also supports the use of stellar cues and learned visual landmarks. The star compass, like the sun compass, is not innate; birds must observe the rotating sky to develop it [N3-R1]. Landmarks and scenery are used for route refinement. The route-memory study states that navigation along habitual routes may be based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks, and pigeons can form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft [N4-F3]. Pigeons are also described as using memorized local features once they become familiar with their environment, and route fidelity varies with landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This shows that learned route memory becomes especially important for familiar areas and short-distance navigation.

## 2) How do compass-based orientation and route-based navigation differ?

Compass-based orientation and route-based navigation serve different navigational functions:

- **Compass-based orientation** provides broad directional heading. It relies on cues such as magnetic inclination, solar position, and celestial cues to maintain overall direction. The evidence indicates that magnetic compass orientation gives poleward/equatorward information, while the sun compass helps birds compensate for the sun’s apparent movement [N2-F1][N3-F2]. This system is useful for long-distance migration and unfamiliar navigation.

- **Route-based navigation** relies on memory of landmarks and scenery to refine the path. Once birds become familiar with an area, they resort to memorized local features rather than relying solely on compass cues [N4-F3]. This means route memory is not a substitute for compass orientation; it is a refinement mechanism that helps birds stay on a specific path after they have learned it.

The distinction is important because birds do not switch between one system and the other in isolation. Instead, the evidence suggests that compass orientation gives the general direction, while landmarks and scenery stabilize the route and allow birds to adjust heading when they are near home [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3]. The review also notes that the role of magnetic parameters in position finding is poorly understood, and that experiments reveal enormous variability, which underscores the complexity of integrating multiple cues [N2-F1].

## 3) How do birds combine different cues to maintain heading and position?

Birds combine cues in a multimodal, interrelated way. The evidence shows that magnetic and celestial cues interact in complex ways, with transfers of information between them demonstrated [N2-F1]. The sun compass review explains that the time-compensated sun compass is central to navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process, and that solar cues may also function as heading indicators or even contribute to place recognition [N3-F2]. This means that birds do not treat each cue as a separate system; instead, they integrate compass information with map-like information to control direction and position.

The route-memory evidence supports the same idea. Pigeons combine compass and landmark guidance in familiar route navigation [N4-R4]. This indicates that multiple cues are used in parallel rather than sequentially. The study also shows that pigeons process their visual environment on a characteristic spatial scale and that route fidelity is influenced by landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This suggests that cue integration is not only about combining compass and landmark information, but also about tuning that combination to the local environment.

The broader evidence on cue integration also implies that birds reduce error by using multiple cues. Although the evidence provided is thinner on this point than on the specific cue systems, the contextual material on multimodal navigation indicates that navigation is multi-modal, and birds may use different cues at different times in response to environmental conditions [N6-R2]. In other words, birds compensate for uncertainty by relying on a combination of cues rather than a single one.

## 4) What environmental cues guide and stabilize bird navigation?

Birds use a hierarchy of cues that guide and stabilize migration:

### a) Magnetic fields  
The magnetic field is an omnipresent, reliable source of orientational information [N2-F1]. Birds use it as a magnetic compass to distinguish between poleward and equatorward directions, and the geomagnetic field is described as a compass cue in Cataglyphis ant navigation [N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that magnetic parameters may provide position-related information, though the use of magnetic information for position finding remains less clear [N2-F1]. This means magnetic cues are important for both heading and, to some extent, position, especially over long distances.

### b) Solar position  
The sun is a dominant orientation cue, especially for diurnal birds. The time-compensated sun compass is described as a central orientation system, and the sun’s geographical direction does not change with the animal’s position [N3-F2]. The review also notes that solar-derived cues may function as heading indicators and that shadows can contribute to navigation in ways that depend on position [N3-F2]. This means solar cues are especially useful for maintaining heading and for fine-scale navigation.

### c) Star patterns  
The evidence shows that birds use stars as a compass, and the star compass is not innate but must be learned through observation of the rotating sky [N3-R1]. While the evidence is less detailed than for the sun compass, this still supports the idea that stellar cues are an important directional cue, especially for nocturnal navigation.

### d) Landmarks and scenery  
Landmarks and scenery stabilize familiar routes. The evidence states that navigation along habitual routes may be based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks, and pigeons can form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft [N4-F3]. Route memory is also linked to landscape complexity: pigeons form route memories most strongly in regions with moderate landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This means that landmarks and scenery are not just passive cues; they are actively used to refine the path and maintain route fidelity.

## 5) Which cues are used at different migration stages and distances?

The evidence supports a staged navigation strategy:

- **Long-distance migration and unfamiliar navigation** rely heavily on map-like compass systems. The magnetic orientation review says that birds are sensitive to the Earth’s magnetic field and its variations, and that magnetic compass orientation is part of a multifactorial navigational system [N2-F1]. The sun compass review describes the time-compensated sun compass as central to navigation from unfamiliar places in a two-step map-and-compass process [N3-F2]. This suggests that long-distance migrants use broad compass and map-like information to maintain direction over large distances.

- **Familiar-route navigation** relies more on learned landmarks and scenery. Once birds become familiar with their environment, they resort to memorized local features [N4-F3]. Pigeons are described as using memorized local features once they are familiar with their surroundings, and their route fidelity is influenced by landscape complexity [N4-F3]. This indicates that learned route memory becomes more prominent when birds are navigating from places they have visited before.

- **Route fidelity and memory formation** depend on repeated travel and experience. The evidence shows that pigeons are released repeatedly from the same site and that this repeated exposure leads to the formation of memorized paths [N4-F3]. Route fidelity varies greatly within individual routes, between individuals, between sites, and even between lofts [N4-F3], showing that memory formation is shaped by experience rather than being fixed.

## 6) What disturbances can disrupt navigation?

Bird navigation is vulnerable to several disturbances:

### a) Natural disturbances  
Geomagnetic disturbances are a major concern. The evidence states that geomagnetic disturbances affect the navigation of both young birds and their elders, suggesting that birds rely similarly on geomagnetism [N5-R1]. It also reports that geomagnetic disturbances are associated with increased incidence of wrong-way bird migrations [N5-R4]. A magnetic storm study notes that solar activity can alter the geomagnetic field at unpredictable intervals, disrupting temporal geomagnetic variations during migration [N5-F4]. This means that birds can be thrown off course by geomagnetic variability.

### b) Weather and magnetic interference  
Weather-related geomagnetic variability can disrupt the perception of magnetic information during migration [N5-F4]. Magnetic anomalies caused by the Earth’s crust can also disrupt navigation ability [N2-F1]. The evidence suggests that birds may reduce activity when magnetic information is disrupted, as the European robin reduced nocturnal migratory restlessness in response to simulated solar storms [N5-F4]. This indicates that birds do not always maintain orientation under disturbance; instead, they may alter behavior when cues are unreliable.

### c) Human-made and light-related disturbances  
Although the evidence is thinner on light pollution than on geomagnetic disturbances, the broader context of celestial cues and the sun compass implies that artificial light could disrupt nocturnal orientation. The sun compass review notes that clock shift experiments are ambiguous indicators of sun compass use [N3-F2], which suggests that disruptions to circadian or sky-based cues can interfere with navigation. The evidence also implies that light pollution may disrupt nocturnal orientation by altering the availability or reliability of celestial cues [N3-F2].

### d) What happens when cues are unreliable or missing  
When navigation cues are unreliable or missing, birds may drift off course, take wrong-way routes, or fail to maintain consistent heading. The evidence shows that geomagnetic disturbances can cause wrong-way migrations [N5-R4], and that birds may rely on the same geomagnetic cues even when displaced, suggesting that cue loss can force them to rely more heavily on other cues or to become disoriented [N5-R1][N5-F4]. The review on magnetic orientation also notes that the role of magnetic parameters in navigation is poorly understood, with experiments revealing enormous variability and the need for magnetic recalibration [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that navigation becomes less reliable when cues are inconsistent, and that birds may fail to recalibrate or compensate effectively under disturbance.

## 7) How do birds learn routes and use memory during migration?

Birds learn routes through repeated travel and experience. The evidence shows that pigeons are able to learn and subsequently follow habitual routes home, with navigation along these routes based on the recognition of memorized visual landmarks [N4-F3]. The study also notes that pigeons may form idiosyncratic memorized paths to the home loft, which they recapitulate even after being released from a short distance from the original site [N4-F3]. This indicates that route memory is not just a single memory but a learned path that can be recalled repeatedly.

Repeated travel and experience are critical to route fidelity. The evidence indicates that pigeons are released repeatedly from the same site and that this repeated exposure leads to the formation of memorized paths [N4-F3]. Route fidelity increases with repeated release, and the study reports that route formation and route fidelity vary greatly within individual routes, between individuals, between sites, and even between lofts [N4-F3]. This suggests that experience shapes memory formation, and that route memory is strengthened by repeated exposure.

Landscape complexity affects route memory and navigation by determining whether memory can be formed and retained effectively. The evidence shows that pigeons form route memories most strongly in regions where landscape complexity is neither too great nor too low [N4-F3]. The study concludes that pigeons process their visual environment on a characteristic spatial scale and that landscape complexity is a key predictor of fidelity to the habitual route [N4-F3]. This means that overly complex landscapes may overwhelm the bird’s memory system, while overly simple landscapes may not provide enough structure to support route learning. The evidence also notes that pigeons are attracted to strong linear features in the landscape, such as roads and rivers, and that landmarks influence flight path structure [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that landscape complexity influences which landmarks become salient and how effectively a route can be remembered and followed.

## 8) Integrated conclusion

In ecology, birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration through a combination of innate compass systems, celestial cues, and learned route memory. They use the magnetic field as a compass to distinguish direction, the sun as a time-compensated compass to maintain heading, and stars as a nocturnal compass [N2-F1][N3-F2][N3-R1]. Landmarks and scenery provide route refinement and familiar navigation, especially once birds become accustomed to an area [N4-F3]. Birds also integrate cues across stages: long-distance migration depends on map-like orientation, while familiar routes depend on memory of landmarks and scenery [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

Disturbances such as geomagnetic storms, solar variability, magnetic anomalies, weather, and artificial light can disrupt navigation by degrading cue reliability or making cues unavailable [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-F4]. When cues are unreliable or missing, birds may fail to maintain heading, drift off course, or take wrong-way routes [N5-R4][N5-F4]. Learning and memory are therefore critical: repeated travel strengthens route memory, and birds’ ability to remember familiar routes depends on the structure of the landscape and the balance between too much and too little visual information [N4-F3].

Overall, bird migration is a sophisticated ecological achievement that depends on a flexible, multimodal navigation system, with cues selected and integrated depending on the migration stage, distance, and environmental conditions [N2-F1][N3-F2][N6-R2]. Birds do not rely on a single cue; they combine compass, celestial, and learned route information to achieve precise navigation during migration.
